catalog_quote: For the most part, the Iquito stress system is relatively simple, consisting of right-to-left exhaustively parsed moraic trochees. The language generally does not permit degenerate feet. The language is quantity sensitive, with C(y)V: syllables counting as heavy (recall that the language does not exhibit closed syllables). [p. 57] ... (5) a. (ˈLL) i. (ˈa.ʃi) 'bird sp.' ... c. (ˌLL)(ˈLL) i. (ˌku.ma)(ˈki.ha) 'suri (edible beetle grub)' ... e. (ˌLL)(ˌLL)(ˈLL) i. (ˌkana)(ˌnahu)(ˈkura) 'we (excl.) wrote (a few days ago)' ... Turning to words containing heavy syllables, we find that all heavy syllables are stressed in Iquito, and that the stress pattern in such words shows that heavy syllables form their own foot. This indicates that the trochees in the language are moraic, and not syllabic. [p. 58] ... (6) a. nu(ˌta.ku)(ˈrɨɨ) 's/he stood up' b. *(ˌnu.ta)(kuˈrɨɨ) ... (7) a. (ˌii)(ˈpɨɨ) 'Red Howler Monkey' ... Feet are minimally bimoraic, but trimoraic feet are found in the language, as in (8a&b), due to the process of foot formation. ... (8) a. (ˈsaa.pi) 'stingray' b. (ˌmɨɨ.sɨ)(ˈyɨ.ka) 'sacha ajos' ... Note, however, that the language does not permit degenerate feet at the right edge of the word, as in the unattested patterns in (9d&e). [pp. 58-59]

sweep_summary: Iquito (iqui1243) is not in the catalog. All four works with stress in the title are about Iquito word stress. Three were downloaded open and read: Michael 2011 (Amerindia 35, journal site) is the authoritative first-hand statement — quantity-sensitive right-to-left moraic trochees, primary stress on the rightmost foot (penult .LL, final if heavy), all heavy syllables stressed, left-edge degenerate feet only to make a dipodic word, stress diagnosed by post-tonic consonant lengthening and separated from a low-density H/ø tone system whose default H docks on the stressed syllable. Sullón Acosta 2005 (UNMSM thesis, recovered via the DSpace 7 backend at handle 20.500.12672/1230; Glottolog's URL is dead) equates 'primary stress' with the pitch peak and so places it toward the left edge (LEFTMOST ranking) with penultimate 'secondary stress'; Michael 2011 p. 71 rejects that premise, and her right-to-left footing and penultimate prominence agree with his analysis once pitch is reassigned to tone. Topintzi 2017 (ISTAL 22, open) is a Harmonic-Serialism reanalysis of Michael's data with no new data ('leftward bimoraic trochees with rightmost primary stress'); it points to a fuller chapter, Topintzi 2016 in Dimensions of Phonological Stress (CUP, paywalled, not in the item list). Michael 2010 (Berkeley PLAR) could not be downloaded (eScholarship WAF; Internet Archive offline) and is presumably the prepublication of the 2011 article — low priority. Suggested coding: fixed rightmost-foot (penultimate/final) quantity-sensitive trochaic stress with a separate lexical tone system. all discovery was by direct download.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Feet are bimoraic trochees built from the right edge of the prosodic word; the head of the rightmost foot carries primary stress. So primary stress is penultimate when the last two syllables are light (ˈa.ʃi, ku.ma.ˈki.ha), final when the final syllable has a long vowel (nu.ta.ku.ˈrɨɨ), and on a heavy penult before a light final (ˈsaa.pi, trimoraic foot rather than a final degenerate foot). Every long-vowel syllable is stressed. Primary stress carries a default high tone when the word has no lexical tone in its rightmost colon; the acoustic correlate of stress itself is lengthening of the post-tonic consonant, not pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: exhaustive right-to-left parsing gives secondary stress on the head of every non-final foot, e.g. (ˌkana)(ˌnahu)(ˈkura), (ˌii)(ˈpɨɨ). A single light syllable at the left edge is normally left unparsed, but is parsed into a degenerate secondary-stressed foot when that makes the word dipodic: (ˌka)(ˈha.ʃi) 'hair', (ˌma)(ˈhuu). Degenerate feet are never permitted at the right edge (*(ˌL)(ˈL), *(ˌH)(ˈL)).
new_statements.exceptions: Trimoraic feet (ˈHL) at the right edge; degenerate initial feet in trisyllabic/dipodic words. Michael notes Sullón (2005) analyzed the same data with primary stress on the leftmost foot by equating primary stress with the pitch peak, and Eastman & Eastman (1963) posited tone but no stress; he attributes both to conflating pitch with stress. The 2019/2022 dictionaries report a revised tonal analysis (H/L/null, HLL melodies) but do not revise the stress statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word, defined (fn. 1, p. 66) as the domain of stress and tone assignment and the unit subject to the bimoraic minimum; monomoraic pronouns and negation cliticize into the host's prosodic word (nu=makii, ka=tɨ=ʃiipa). Transcriptions are non-prepausal citation forms (prepausal final-vowel devoicing and long-vowel shortening do not affect stress). Data from San Antonio de Pintuyacu speakers, 2002-2008; stress established by tapping tasks plus post-tonic consonant duration.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the Iquito of San Antonio de Pintuyacu (Pintuyacu River, Loreto), the only community with fluent speakers; language-level iqui1243. Michael 2011 (p. 54) notes Kawarano, sometimes listed separately, is considered a dialect of Iquito by speakers.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the prepublication version of the Amerindia 35 (2011) article already in existing_statements: the §4 text is word-for-word the same apart from 'C(y)V: vowels' (2010) vs 'C(y)V: syllables' (2011), and examples (5)-(10) and Table 3 are identical. It adds nothing beyond the 2011 statement but independently confirms it; it also fills the catalog record's empty 'rule' field with the weight-sensitive moraic-trochee rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive right-to-left moraic trochees, exhaustively parsed: primary stress on the head of the rightmost foot, so on the penult in words ending in two light (CV) syllables (e.g. (ˌkuma)(ˈkiha)) and on a final heavy CV: syllable, which forms its own foot (nu(ˌtaku)(ˈrɨɨ)); every heavy syllable is stressed; a final..HL string is parsed as a trimoraic (ˈHL) foot rather than a final degenerate foot ((ˈsaa.pi)). Stress is identified by two tapping tasks (strongest syllable = primary stress; any strong syllable = any stress) and by lengthening of the post-tonic consonant, not by pitch; metrical H tone is assigned to the primary-stressed syllable in words lacking lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the head of every non-final foot, alternating leftward: (ˌkana)(ˌnahu)(ˈkura) 'we (excl.) wrote', nu(ˌniki)(ˌkɨkɨ)(ˈkura) 's/he trembled'; a single left-edge light syllable takes secondary stress as a degenerate foot only when that makes the word dipodic ((ˌka)(ˈha.ʃi) 'hair', (ˌma)(ˈhuu)).
new_statements.exceptions: Degenerate (monomoraic) feet are otherwise banned and never allowed at the right edge (*(ˌL)(ˈL), *(ˌH)(ˈL)); trimoraic (HL) feet arise instead of a final degenerate foot; a leftover initial light syllable is left unparsed when the word is already dipodic (nu(ˌtaki)(ˈnaka)); monomoraic function words cliticize or lengthen to meet the bimoraic minimum. §6 (p. 75) rejects Sullón's (2005) pitch-peak-based stress analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Michael 2010 describes the Iquito of San Antonio de Pintuyacu (ILDP fieldwork, the same community as the 2011 article); no other dialect is at issue.

tone_statements.citation: Beier, Christine (2023). Documenting and describing tone in Iquito: a progress report. Talk, Phorum (UC Berkeley Phonetics and Phonology Forum), 1 September 2023. Abstract published on the Phorum 2023 programme page, UC Berkeley Department of Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: Despite being the only member of its family known to exhibit tone, and despite occurring in a part of the world reported to have only a modest density of tone languages, which in turn are said to exhibit, by-and-large, simple tone systems, Iquito turns out to be a tone powerhouse, exhibiting a H, L, Ø (underlying and surface) tone inventory; (usually HLL) lexical melodies and (always H) boundary tones; both rightward and leftward tone spreading; both linked and floating tones; both fixed and mobile melodies; and various morphological and constructional (grammatical) melodies, all integrated via dominance relations among the many domains involved in word and utterance formation.

NEH Dynamic Language Infrastructure - Documenting Endangered Languages Fellowship, 2022 (Regents of the University of California, Berkeley; outright $60,000; project period June 2022 - August 2023). Project description published in 'NEH DEL Fellowship awarded to Beier', UC Berkeley Linguistics news, 26 April 2022; award listed in NEH 'Grant awards April 2022, state by state', California/Berkeley.
tone_statements.quote: This project advances the documentation and description of Iquito, a critically endangered Zaparoan language of northern Peruvian Amazonia, with a focus on its complex tonal system. Core activities include transcription, parsing, and analysis of texts from circa 1960; re-parsing of re-analyzed texts from 2002-2018; and comparative analysis of these texts to inform ongoing grammatical description of Iquito. Because Iquito's tonal system includes both boundary Hs and HLL melodies that surface in multiple domains and across word boundaries, text-based analysis of connected speech is an indispensable tool for discovery. Thorough documentation of Iquito’s tonal system will inform the typology of tone in Amazonia, and contribute to cross-linguistic typology and theories of grammatical tone.
tone_statements.locator: Beier's quoted project description, paragraph 2 of the news item
tone_statements.summary: Tone-and-stress language; tonal system with boundary H tones and HLL tonal melodies realised over several morphological domains and across word boundaries (project description; details in Beier 2023 Phorum abstract listed here earlier).

sources.citation: Sullón Acosta, Karina Natalia (2005). El acento y tono en la lengua Iquito. Tesis de Licenciatura, Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos, Lima. vi+97 pp. (110 pp. PDF).
sources.quote: p. 4: 'a. El acento primario recae sobre la sílaba que esté más a la izquierda de la palabra prosódica, siempre y cuando la sílaba que le sigue sea ligera. b. Acentúese la segunda sílaba si ésta es pesada. En el caso de palabras de tres y cuatro sílabas asígnese el acento en la segunda sílaba, siempre y cuando la primera sílaba sea ligera. c. Asígnese el acento sobre la tercera sílaba en el caso de palabras de cinco sílabas, siempre y cuando las dos anteriores sean ligeras.' p. 87: 'El pitch alto es un rasgo de acento primario en iquito y éste se asigna mediante la formación de pies desde el margen derecho de la palabra. No obstante, la cabeza de la palabra prosódica es el pie que está más a la izquierda.' [Translation: a. Primary stress falls on the leftmost syllable of the prosodic word provided the following syllable is light. b. Stress the second syllable if it is heavy; in three- and four-syllable words assign stress to the second syllable provided the first is light. c. Assign stress to the third syllable in five-syllable words whenever the two preceding ones are light. / High pitch is a feature of primary stress in Iquito and it is assigned by foot formation from the right…
sources.note: Resumen pp. 2-7 and §4.4 pp. 54-60: two prominences per word (one near the left edge, one penultimate); takes high pitch as the correlate of primary stress, so primary stress falls on the leftmost foot (first syllable if the next is light; second syllable if heavy or in 3-4 syllable words with light first syllable; third syllable in 5-syllable words), secondary stress always penultimate; a 'fourth pattern' with initial stress regardless of weight, attributed to a lexical low tone; verbs stress the heavy root syllable. Michael 2011 §6 (p. 71) rejects this pitch-based analysis.

sources.citation: Topintzi, Nina (2017). The prosodic colon in stress, tone and prosodic templates: Evidence from Iquito and elsewhere. Selected Papers of ISTAL 22: 466-479.
sources.quote: Iquito, a Zaparoan language of Peru (all data come from Michael 2011) is a low-density tonal language that displays both stress and tone. [...] Iquito parses feet into leftward bimoraic trochees with rightmost primary stress. These can either contain a single heavy syllable (H) or two light ones (LL). [...] Iquito normally bans degenerate (L) feet [...] In odd-parity words [...] the extra syllable at the left edge of the word remains unparsed.
sources.note: Secondary (all data from Michael 2011): 'Iquito parses feet into leftward bimoraic trochees with rightmost primary stress' (p. 468); Harmonic Serialism analysis of the degenerate-foot/colon facts.

sources.note: Analysis of Iquito 'mobile tonal melodies', i.e. tonal melodies whose position is affected by adjacent words or adjacent morphemes; position argued to follow from an interaction between positional faithfulness and a preference for underlying tones to be realized on the surface; generalizations depended on tonal behaviour in connected discourse (texts) as well as elicitation.

sources.citation: Michael, Lev (2003 [CV: 2004]). La fusión fonológica en el idioma Iquito (Familia Záparo, Amazonía peruana) / Phonological fusion in Iquito (Zaparoan). Memorias del Congreso de Idiomas Indígenas de Latinoamérica-I (CILLA I, University of Texas at Austin, October 2003). Austin: AILLA/CILLA.

tone.quote: Los criterios que he utilizado para determinar si dos palabras son o no fusionadas en el idioma Iquito son los siguientes: 1. Supresión de una vocal, o formación de una semivocal, al lindero de las palabras fusionadas en el caso que la fusión resultaría en un núcleo silábico prohibido (véase a Huamancayo Curi (2003)) 2. Las palabras fusionadas comparten un sólo acento principal [...] Nuestros estudios de patrones de acentuación en Iquito sugieren que el pie prosódico es bimoraico, y por eso, es muy probable que los procesos que aumentan el tamaño de palabras monomoraicas son impulsados por un requisito inviolable que pies prosódicos deben tener dos moras.
tone.locator: §2 'Palabras Gramaticales y Palabras Fonológicas', fusion criteria, p. 2; §3.2 'La fusión prosódica de palabras monomoraicas', p. 6; conditioning by lexical stress §3.1, p. 5
tone.translation: The criteria I have used to determine whether or not two words are fused in Iquito are the following: 1. Deletion of a vowel, or formation of a glide, at the boundary of the fused words in case fusion would yield a prohibited syllable nucleus (see Huamancayo Curi 2003) 2. The fused words share a single primary stress [...] Our studies of stress patterns in Iquito suggest that the prosodic foot is bimoraic, and therefore it is very likely that the processes that increase the size of monomoraic words are driven by an inviolable requirement that prosodic feet must have two moras.
